C1.quote: One of my goals for Python was to make it so that all objects were "first class." By this, I meant that I wanted all objects that could be named in the language ... to have equal status.
C1.statement: Make every object that can be named a first-class citizen with equal status: assignable, passable, storable, callable. (instead of: reserving special status for functions, classes or types so some things can be named but not handled like the rest)

C2.quote: I decided that there should be no undefined result values in Python – instead, exceptions should always be raised when no correct return value can be computed.
C2.statement: Never return an undefined or silently wrong value; raise an exception whenever no correct result can be computed. (instead of: returning sentinels, undefined values or silently wrapped results that let an error pass unnoticed)

C3.quote: This is one area where Python violated the ABC-inspired philosophy of not requiring users to care about a uninteresting implementation details.
C3.statement: Don't make users care about uninteresting implementation details. (instead of: requiring markers, suffixes or declarations that exist only to serve the implementation)

C4.quote: I decided to generalize these to a common concept, the sequence. This generalization made it so certain core operations such as getting the length (len(s)), indexing (s[i]), slicing (s[i:j]), and iteration (for i in s) worked the same on any sequence type.
C4.statement: When several types share operations, generalize them to one common concept so the same operations work the same on all. (instead of: giving each type its own separate operations with their own names and behavior)

C5.quote: A major design constraint was that I didn't want to add syntax for methods that differed from the syntax for functions. Refactoring the grammar and the byte code generator to handle such similar cases differently felt like a huge task.
C5.statement: Prefer the minimal solution that reuses existing constructs; don't add new syntax when an existing one will do. (instead of: inventing dedicated syntax for each new feature (a method keyword, operator declarations, a metaclass clause))

C6.quote: One of the rules I took from ABC was that every data type, when printed or converted to a string, should be represented by an expression that was a valid input to the language's parser.
C6.statement: Make a value's printed representation an expression that is valid input to the parser. (instead of: printing values in an ad-hoc display form that can't be read back as code)

C7.quote: the invariant that when two / slices are adjacent, the first slice's end index is the second slice's / start index is just too beautiful to ignore.
C7.statement: Choose the convention whose invariant makes the common cases come out clean, without +1/-1 corrections. (instead of: 1-based indexing with closed intervals that force awkward +1/-1 compensation on everyday slicing)
